name: USGS Artificial Intelligence Strategy and AI Research for Earth Science
title: USGS Artificial Intelligence Strategy and AI Research for Earth Science
answer: The U.S. Geological Survey publishes an artificial intelligence strategy and a body of AI research covering geospatial machine learning, satellite operations and mineral and energy mapping. Its most useful single item for mining readers is the strategy itself, which commits the Bureau to building an AI workforce, AI governance, trustworthy use, modern computing infrastructure and faster adoption, and notes that staff had already used AI in workflows for years without a comprehensive strategy.

sections.body: This is the U.S. Geological Survey website, read across sixty pages in October 2026. It includes a publication record for the 'Artificial intelligence strategy for the U.S. Geological Survey', overview pages from the Center of Excellence for Geospatial Information Science, the Science Analytics and Synthesis program and the Science Synthesis, Analysis, and Research program, two episodes of the Eyes on Earth podcast on AI at the EROS data centre, and publication records for machine learning research in geoscience, geothermal energy and hydrological illustration. The material is a mix of strategy, plain language explanation and peer reviewed research summaries.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The strategy is motivated by rapid AI development, the benefits of adoption to USGS mission delivery, public concern about trustworthiness, and emerging Federal directives. Its vision is to keep integrating AI for public good science while maintaining ethics, scientific integrity and compliance with Federal and Department of the Interior requirements. Five steps follow: develop a strong AI workforce, adapt organisational approaches to include AI governance and communication, ensure responsible and trustworthy use, modernise computing and data infrastructure, and accelerate adoption and innovation. The Bureau notes staff adopted AI in workflows for many years without a comprehensive strategy. Elsewhere the site explains AI in plain terms, covering feature extraction, pattern recognition, natural language processing, machine learning, ontologies and foundations, and describes CEGIS using machine learning to map terrain features and analyse landscapes. Podcast episodes describe AI as increasingly necessary at EROS, credit it with making the National Land Cover Database an annual product, and discuss training algorithms on satellite subcomponent measurements, debris and orbital rates for collision avoidance and fuel saving. Research records compare machine learning methods for geothermal favourability mapping and set out a supervised learning workflow to bridge geoscience and machine learning vocabulary.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that the term AI was coined in 1956 and that early methodologies were dominated by rules based systems. It says Landsat satellites fly at a consistent 705 kilometre altitude and that Landsats 8 and 9 generate thousands of subcomponent measurements. In the geothermal study, nine favourability maps were compared, six built with logistic regression, XGBoost and support vector machines under two training strategies, one with an artificial neural network, and two using expert decision methods from the 2008 assessment. F1 scores were below 0.10 for all approaches and did not improve with model complexity, which the authors attribute to limitations in the input features. CEGIS hosted its annual research meeting on 22 to 24 July 2025 and scheduled the eighteenth meeting for 23 to 25 June 2026 in Denver, Colorado.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in mining gets a documented national strategy for AI in a public earth science agency, which shows how a large geological organisation governs, staffs and funds AI rather than only experimenting with it. The research records are directly relevant to mineral and energy prospectivity work, since they compare machine learning methods against expert driven favourability mapping and warn that model complexity cannot compensate for weak input features. The EROS material shows operational AI uses in satellite health monitoring and collision avoidance, the infrastructure that underpins the remote sensing datasets mining analysts rely on.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Mining

sections.body: The site is a government science agency's own account and does not address mining companies, mineral extraction or commercial prospectivity. The strategy publication record gives goals and motivations but no budget, timetable or performance measures. The podcast pages are episode summaries rather than transcripts. The geothermal study concerns geothermal resources, not minerals, and its authors report weak results limited by training data. Several pages are programme overviews that mention AI only in passing, and the CEGIS pages repeat the same explanatory text.
